faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Short, direct answers to the questions people ask most about Parallax.

general.question: What is Parallax?
general.answer: Parallax is a proof-of-work blockchain with Bitcoin's monetary rules and the Ethereum Virtual Machine. Supply is capped at 21 million LAX, a block arrives about every 10 minutes, and the block subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks. Smart contracts written for Ethereum run on it, up to the Paris fork.

general.question: Who created Parallax?
general.answer: It doesn't matter — and that is the point. The source code was public before launch, the launch date was announced in advance, and the supply at genesis was zero, so every participant stood at the same starting line. The original authors hold no keys to the protocol, received no allocation, and are required for nothing; the network would not notice their disappearance. Every claim about Parallax can be checked against the chain itself, so authorship carries no authority.

general.question: How is Parallax different from Bitcoin and Ethereum?
general.answer: It takes its monetary policy from Bitcoin: a 21 million cap, 10-minute blocks, halvings every 210,000 blocks and proof of work. It takes the EVM from Ethereum, so it runs smart contracts that Bitcoin can't. Unlike today's Ethereum, it is mined rather than staked, its supply is fixed, and no fees are burned: the miner keeps the whole fee.

general.question: Why Proof of Work instead of Proof of Stake?
general.answer: Proof of work ties security to an external cost, energy, that can't be simulated, voted into existence or negotiated. Proof of stake hands control to whoever holds the most coins, which moves trust to validators instead of removing it. Under proof of work, influence over the chain has to be paid for with work. It can't be granted by holdings or identity.

general.question: How do I add Parallax to MetaMask?
general.answer: Add a custom network in MetaMask with these values: network name Parallax, RPC URL https://rpc.parallaxprotocol.org, chain ID 2110, currency symbol LAX, block explorer https://explorer.parallaxprotocol.org. The Wallets page can also add it in one click. Other EVM wallets take the same values.

technical.question: What consensus mechanism does Parallax use?
technical.answer: Proof of work, with the XHash algorithm. XHash is memory-hard and mined on GPUs, unlike Bitcoin's SHA-256, which is dominated by ASICs.

technical.question: What is XHash and why was it chosen?
technical.answer: XHash is a modified Ethash variant: memory-hard, so commodity GPUs mine competitively, and altered precisely so that the existing stock of Ethash ASICs cannot be reused on Parallax. A proof-of-work network is most fragile in its early years, when total hashrate is small; XHash ensures that security in those years is supplied by widely held hardware rather than by whoever owns the residue of another chain's hardware arms race.

technical.question: Is Parallax EVM compatible?
technical.answer: Yes — Parallax runs the Ethereum Virtual Machine, complete through the Paris fork. Contracts written in Solidity or Vyper deploy unchanged, and familiar tools like MetaMask, Remix, Hardhat, and Foundry work with only a chain ID change (2110). One caveat: opcodes introduced after Paris (such as PUSH0 from Shanghai) are not available, so set your compiler's EVM version to "paris" — Solidity 0.8.20 and later targets Shanghai by default.

technical.question: What are the block times and transaction fees?
technical.answer: A block arrives about every 10 minutes. Difficulty is retargeted every block with ASERT (two-day half-life), so the interval stays close to 10 minutes as hashrate comes and goes. Fees are a plain gas-price auction: there is no EIP-1559 base fee, miners include the highest-paying transactions first, and the whole fee goes to the miner.

technical.question: How many confirmations should I wait for?
technical.answer: It depends on the amount. Each confirmation adds about 10 minutes of work that an attacker would have to redo. One or two confirmations is usually enough for small payments; Bitcoin's convention of six (about an hour) is a sensible default for larger ones. Parallax is a young proof-of-work network with far less hashrate than Bitcoin, so wait longer for large transfers, and check status.parallaxprotocol.org for reorgs or incidents before you treat a payment as final.

technical.question: Why 10-minute blocks instead of faster?
technical.answer: Global agreement takes physical time. Systems that push time-to-finality below physical limits create hidden advantages: proximity to other miners, specialized networking, privileged transaction ordering. Each of these centralizes consensus. Parallax treats time as a stabilizing force: finality earned slowly through accumulated work is more robust than finality declared quickly by agreement.

technical.question: What is the block gas limit?
technical.answer: 600 million gas per block. At one block every 10 minutes that is about 1 million gas per second, less than Ethereum's mainnet. The limit is kept low on purpose so that a full node stays cheap to run on ordinary hardware.

technical.question: How does Parallax handle 51% attacks?
technical.answer: Like any proof-of-work chain, Parallax can be reorganized by someone with a majority of the hashrate. What stands in the way is cost: rewriting history means redoing more work than the honest chain, and that cost grows with every block. XHash keeps mining on widely owned GPUs and locks out existing Ethash ASICs, and ASERT adjusts difficulty every block, so a sudden swing in hashrate can't distort it for long. Mined rewards can't be spent for 100 blocks, which stops a miner spending coins a reorg could erase. For large amounts, wait for more confirmations.

technical.question: What is coinbase maturity?
technical.answer: Newly mined LAX can't be spent until 100 more blocks have been built on top of it, about 17 hours. If a block is reorganized out of the chain, its reward disappears with it; the wait makes sure nobody has spent that reward in the meantime.

technical.question: What are the hardware requirements for running a full node?
technical.answer: A full node runs on an ordinary computer: 2 or more CPU cores (4 recommended), at least 4 GB of RAM (16 GB recommended), an SSD with 200 GB free (500 GB or more for an archive node) and a stable connection of about 25 Mbit/s. The SSD matters most; hard drives struggle to sync.

mining.question: How can I mine Parallax?
mining.answer: Mine on a GPU with Hashwarp, the official open-source miner, or with SRBMiner-Multi. Point it at a Parallax pool, or at your own node to mine solo. Other Ethash miners such as ethminer do not work. The client also has a built-in CPU miner, but it is only useful for testing.

mining.question: What is the mining reward schedule?
mining.answer: The block subsidy started at 50 LAX and halves every 210,000 blocks, roughly every four years at 10-minute blocks: the same schedule as Bitcoin. The miner also collects every fee in the block. Mined LAX can be spent after 100 blocks.

mining.question: Can I use my Ethereum mining rig?
mining.answer: Yes — the hardware carries over. XHash is Ethash-derived and memory-hard, so Ethash-class GPU rigs mine Parallax competitively without hardware changes. The software does change: existing Ethash miners cannot mine XHash, so use Hashwarp (the official open-source miner) or SRBMiner-Multi, pointed at a Parallax pool or your own node.

economics.question: What is the total supply of Parallax?
economics.answer: 21 million LAX, the same cap as Bitcoin. New supply comes only from the block subsidy, which halves every 210,000 blocks. There was no premine, and there is no governance body that could raise the cap.

economics.question: How are transaction fees handled?
economics.answer: Fees are a first-price auction on gas price. There is no EIP-1559 base fee and nothing is burned: the miner who includes a transaction receives its entire fee.

economics.question: Why doesn't Parallax burn fees like Ethereum?
economics.answer: Burning fees takes income away from the people securing the chain. As halvings shrink the block subsidy, fees become miners' main income, and the network's long-term security depends on them. Paying the whole fee to miners keeps that link intact.

economics.question: What happens when all 21 million coins are mined?
economics.answer: Miners are then paid by fees alone, as in Bitcoin. The subsidy shrinks with every halving, so it takes more than a century to reach zero. Because no fees are burned, all of that fee income goes to the miners securing the chain.

economics.question: Is there a premine or ICO?
economics.answer: No. There was no premine, no ICO, no presale and no allocation to developers. The genesis block held zero LAX, the launch date was announced in advance, and every coin in circulation was mined.

economics.question: Where can I get LAX?
economics.answer: Mine it, or buy it on one of the exchanges listed on the Exchanges page. Exchanges are independent businesses: once you've bought, withdraw to a wallet you control.

governance.question: How are protocol upgrades decided?
governance.answer: There is no roadmap and no schedule of hard forks. The monetary rules (the 21 million cap, the halving schedule and proof of work) are not up for change. Consensus rules are meant to ossify: changes are limited to fixing real defects, and a fix takes effect only if node operators choose to run it. The one consensus change so far, the switch to ASERT difficulty at block 17,560, fixed a retargeting window that miners were manipulating. Ongoing development happens in the client, tooling and contracts, not in the consensus rules.

governance.question: Is there a foundation or company behind Parallax?
governance.answer: No. There is no foundation, no company, no treasury, no council, and no privileged governance tokens. Client development happens in the open, and consensus rules are intended to ossify: changes are limited to technical repair, and even a repair becomes real only through the voluntary adoption of node operators, one by one. The original authors hold no keys and are required for nothing — the protocol must remain correct even if its creators disappear or disagree.

governance.question: Will Parallax support Layer 2 solutions?
governance.answer: The base layer is kept conservative on purpose: it exists to settle, not to impress. Experiments belong on higher layers, where failure doesn't threaten settlement. Because Parallax runs the EVM, rollups and sidechains can anchor to it with ordinary contracts, and building one needs no change to the protocol.

governance.question: Are there bridges to other blockchains?
governance.answer: Bridges are built by independent teams, not by the protocol. Parallax is a standard EVM chain, so existing bridge designs can be deployed on it the same way as on any other. Before you use a bridge, check who controls its contracts and what happens to your funds if it fails.

development.question: How can I build on Parallax?
development.answer: Building on Parallax works like building on Ethereum. Use Solidity, Remix, Hardhat, or Foundry, and deploy with MetaMask or any Web3 wallet connected to the Parallax network (chain ID 2110). Set evmVersion to "paris" in your compiler config — the execution layer is complete through the Paris fork, and Solidity 0.8.20+ otherwise emits PUSH0, which Parallax does not support.

development.question: Is there a testnet?
development.answer: There is no public testnet. For contract development, start the client with --dev, which runs a local single-node chain, then deploy to mainnet when you're ready.

development.question: Are there development grants available?
development.answer: No. There is no foundation or treasury, so there is no grant program. Projects are funded by the people who build and use them.

development.question: What tools and libraries are supported?
development.answer: The usual Ethereum tools work: ethers.js, web3.js, viem, MetaMask, Remix, Hardhat, Foundry and OpenZeppelin contracts. Compile with EVM version "paris"; the execution layer does not include post-Paris opcodes.

doctrine.pageSubtitle: Axioms and commentary defining the constraints under which Parallax exists, independent of adoption, relevance or success.

intro.heading: Axioms and Commentary for Durable Settlement
intro.author: By the Parallax contributors
intro.body1: Inspired by the axiomatic style of The Zurich Axioms, this document defines the non-negotiable constraints under which Parallax exists, followed by commentary explaining their necessity.
intro.body2Line1: The axioms are declarative and immutable.
intro.body2Line2: The commentary is explanatory and non-authoritative.
intro.body3: If commentary and axiom ever diverge, the axiom prevails.

purpose.heading: Purpose
purpose.body1: The Parallax Doctrine exists to make explicit the principles that must remain true regardless of adoption, relevance, or success.
purpose.body3: It defines the conditions under which correctness is preserved in adversarial environments.

scope.heading: On Scope and Intent
scope.body1: Parallax does not assume success. It does not presume adoption, relevance, or dominance. It does not define a destiny, roadmap, or outcome.
scope.body2: This doctrine exists to state the conditions under which correctness is preserved regardless of whether Parallax succeeds or fails.
scope.body3: A system that believes it is meant to win will eventually justify intervention to avoid losing. Parallax rejects this premise.

axioms.title: Physical cost is the only scalable defense against revision
axioms.subtitle: Any system that can be rewritten cheaply will be rewritten.
axioms.commentary:
Digital systems do not escape the physical world. Computation consumes energy, communication traverses space, and verification is bounded by hardware. Parallax anchors consensus to Proof-of-Work because it introduces an external, objective cost that cannot be simulated, voted into existence, or socially negotiated.

Energy expenditure creates asymmetry: honest participation accumulates work incrementally, while attacks require disproportionate cost. Proof-of-Work does not guarantee correctness, but it guarantees that rewriting history is expensive. In adversarial systems, expense is credibility.

axioms.title: Time cannot be compressed without centralization
axioms.subtitle: Global agreement requires delay. Attempts to eliminate it create advantage.
axioms.commentary:
Consensus is not computation; it is coordination. Coordination across a global network is constrained by latency, bandwidth, and verification time. These are not engineering problems to be solved away, but physical limits.

Systems that minimize time-to-finality below these limits introduce hidden advantages: proximity, specialized networking, privileged ordering, or coordination mechanisms. Over time, these advantages compound into control. Parallax treats time as a stabilizing force. Finality earned slowly is more robust than finality declared quickly.

axioms.title: Trust that can be reassigned has not been removed
axioms.subtitle: Replacing institutions with committees or validators does not eliminate trust.
axioms.commentary:
Trustlessness does not mean the absence of trust; it means the minimization of trust assumptions. Many systems merely relocate trust—from banks to validators, from institutions to governance—without removing it.

Parallax minimizes trust by ensuring that validity is independently verifiable, enforcement is mechanical, and correctness does not depend on identity or reputation. A system is trustless not when participants are trustworthy, but when trust is unnecessary.

axioms.title: Any rule that requires interpretation will be captured
axioms.subtitle: Rules must be executable without judgment.
axioms.commentary:
Interpretation introduces discretion. Discretion introduces power. If a rule requires context, intent, or explanation to be applied correctly, enforcement depends on human judgment. Judgment accumulates authority, and authority becomes a point of capture.

Parallax favors rules that can be evaluated deterministically. Ambiguity is not flexibility; it is deferred centralization.

axioms.title: Monetary rules must not respond to circumstance
axioms.subtitle: Flexibility in money is discretion in disguise.
axioms.commentary:
Monetary systems fail not because rules are rigid, but because they are negotiable. Exceptions become precedents; discretion attracts influence.

Parallax treats monetary rules as constraints, not policies. They do not adapt to crises, sentiment, or coordination pressure. Predictability is not convenience—it is the foundation of trust minimization.

axioms.title: Permission is incompatible with ownership
axioms.subtitle: Access that can be revoked is not ownership.
axioms.commentary:
Ownership requires irrevocable access. If participation depends on approval, identity, or delegation, access is conditional. Conditional access implies an authority capable of revocation.

Parallax does not grant access. It defines constraints that anyone may satisfy. Permissionlessness is not openness; it is the absence of gatekeepers.

axioms.title: Systems that depend on cooperation will fail under stress
axioms.subtitle: Adversarial conditions are the default, not the exception.
axioms.commentary:
Parallax assumes rational self-interest, asymmetric information, and persistent incentives to cheat. Security does not emerge from goodwill, but from constraints that make misbehavior ineffective.

A system that requires cooperation to remain secure is not decentralized; it is fragile.

axioms.title: History must be expensive to change, not impossible to discuss
axioms.subtitle: Finality emerges from cost, not decree.
axioms.commentary:
History is valuable only if it resists revision. Parallax does not claim absolute immutability; it ensures that rewriting history requires real expenditure.

Absolute immutability is brittle. Cost-based immutability scales. Finality accumulates through work.

axioms.title: The base layer exists to settle, not to impress
axioms.subtitle: Complexity belongs above settlement.
axioms.commentary:
The base layer establishes ordering and finality. Attempting to maximize throughput or expressiveness at this layer increases complexity and attack surface.

Parallax confines experimentation to higher layers, where failure does not threaten settlement integrity. The base layer remains slow, conservative, and difficult to change by design.

axioms.title: Neutral systems must not adapt to narrative
axioms.subtitle: Preference is a form of capture.
axioms.commentary:
Neutrality is not a moral stance; it is an architectural requirement. Parallax applies the same rules regardless of participant, transaction, or context.

Systems that adapt to political, social, or economic narratives introduce discretion. Discretion is the root of capture.

axioms.title: Hidden failure modes compound silently
axioms.subtitle: What cannot be observed cannot be corrected.
axioms.commentary:
Systems that obscure trade-offs, abstract costs, or mask fragility accumulate hidden risk. Failure compounds until collapse.

Parallax favors explicit costs, visible attacks, and acknowledged limitations. Transparency is not optimism; it is resilience.

axioms.title: The protocol must outlive its creators
axioms.subtitle: No individual or organization is required for validity.
axioms.commentary:
Parallax must remain correct even if its creators disappear, disagree, or are forgotten. Intent does not matter. Authority does not matter.

Only validity matters. A system that requires stewardship to survive is not neutral infrastructure.

axioms.title: Infrastructure succeeds by becoming invisible
axioms.subtitle: Longevity, not adoption, is the measure of success.
axioms.commentary:
Parallax is not designed to attract attention, optimize engagement, or chase relevance. Its purpose is to persist.

Longevity requires restraint. Restraint requires constraint. Infrastructure succeeds when it fades into the background.

closing.heading: Closing
closing.body1: Parallax does not ask to be believed.
closing.body2: If any axiom is false, Parallax will fail — and that failure is acceptable.
closing.body4: Parallax is not designed to be liked, upgraded, or governed — only to remain correct.

howItWorks.pageSubtitle: What actually happens when you hold, send and mine LAX, explained without the jargon and with the real numbers.

keys.heading: Your wallet is a key, not an account
keys.subtitle: No company holds your balance. Your coins sit on a public ledger, and only the holder of one secret number can move them.
keys.oneWay: Easy to compute this way. Infeasible to reverse.

privateKey.label: Private key
privateKey.note: A random 256-bit number. Whoever knows it controls the coins. Never share it.

publicKey.label: Public key
publicKey.note: Derived from the private key. Lets anyone check your signatures.

address.label: Address
address.note: A short fingerprint of the public key. Share it to get paid.

points.title: Nobody issues it
points.description: Your wallet generates the key on your own device. No signup, no approval, no account that someone can close.

points.title: The recovery phrase is the key
points.description: Most wallets write the key out as 12 or 24 words. Lose them and the coins are gone for good; anyone who sees them can take the coins.

points.title: Same format as Ethereum
points.description: Addresses look like Ethereum's 0x… addresses, so existing wallets and hardware signers work. The same key controls the same address on both chains, so check which network you are on before sending.

tx.heading: What happens when you press Send
tx.subtitle: A payment reaches every node on the network in seconds, then waits for a miner to write it into the chain.

steps.title: Sign
steps.description: Your wallet builds the transaction (recipient, amount, fee) and signs it with your private key. The key never leaves your device.

steps.title: Broadcast
steps.description: The signed transaction goes to a node, which passes it to its peers. Within seconds the whole network has it.

steps.title: Mempool
steps.description: Each node checks the signature and the balance, then holds the transaction in its waiting room: the mempool.

steps.title: Mined into a block
steps.description: A miner picks transactions, highest fee first, and finds a valid proof-of-work. The new block goes out to every node.

steps.title: Confirmed
steps.description: Every block built on top adds a confirmation. The deeper a transaction sits, the harder it is to undo.

tx.feeBody: You choose a gas price. Miners fill blocks with the best-paying transactions first, and the whole fee goes to the miner. There is no base fee and nothing is burned. When blocks have room, a low fee gets in.
tx.confirmBody: Blocks average ten minutes but don't arrive like clockwork: some come after one minute, some after twenty. Now and then two miners find a block at the same moment and the network briefly splits. It settles on the branch that gets more work on top, and transactions in the losing block go back to the mempool. Every block stacked on yours makes reversing it more expensive.

mining.heading: Miners compete to write the next block
mining.subtitle: Miners repeat one computation over and over, looking for a rare lucky result. Finding one takes enormous work; checking it takes any node a fraction of a second.

loop.title: The mining loop
loop.no: No: change the nonce, try again

mining.reward: The winner collects the block subsidy plus every fee in the block, spendable after 100 more blocks.
mining.xhashBody: Parallax's proof-of-work. Memory-hard and derived from Ethash, but changed so existing Ethash ASICs can't run it. It runs on ordinary GPUs with Hashwarp, the official miner, or SRBMiner-Multi.
mining.asertBody: When miners join, blocks come faster; when they leave, slower. After every block, ASERT compares the chain with its ten-minute schedule and re-tunes the difficulty. For every two days the chain runs ahead of schedule, difficulty doubles; for every two days behind, it halves. Small drift gets small corrections, so block times stay near ten minutes whatever the hashrate does.
mining.chartNote: Blocks speed up for a while, then ASERT raises the difficulty until they are back on schedule.

supply.heading: Where new LAX comes from
supply.subtitle: Every LAX in existence was paid to a miner for a block. There was no premine and no sale: supply at genesis was zero.

facts.label: Subsidy per block in the first era
Blocks between halvings, about four years
Blocks before newly mined coins can move

supply.fees: As the subsidy shrinks, fees take over. Miners keep every fee in full, so in the long run the network's security is paid for by the people using it, not by new coins.

contracts.heading: Programs that hold money
contracts.subtitle: Parallax runs the Ethereum Virtual Machine. A contract is code stored on the chain that can hold LAX and moves it only by its own rules.
rules: Release it to the seller when the buyer confirms delivery
Refund the buyer if nothing happens in 30 days

points.title: Runs exactly as written
points.description: Every node runs the same code and must get the same result. Nobody can change a deployed contract unless its own code allows it.

points.title: Paid for in gas
points.description: Each step of computation costs gas, paid in LAX at the gas price you choose, like any other transaction.

points.title: Ethereum's tools
points.description: Solidity, Hardhat, Foundry and MetaMask all work. The EVM matches Ethereum's through the Paris upgrade.

nodes.heading: Every node checks everything
nodes.subtitle: A full node downloads every block and re-checks every rule itself. It doesn't trust miners, other nodes, or this website.
checks: The miner took no more than the subsidy plus fees
Every contract call gives the same result
nodes.valid: All pass: added to the chain
nodes.invalid: Any fail: rejected, however much work went into it
nodes.noVoteBody: Nodes don't vote and miners don't set the rules. Each node follows the valid chain with the most work behind it. A block that breaks a rule is rejected by every node that checks it, no matter how much hashpower produced it. That is why a majority can't change the rules.

parallaxForBitcoiners.pageSubtitle: Everything Bitcoin fixed, Parallax keeps: 21 million coins, proof-of-work, ten-minute blocks, a launch with no premine. What it adds is the half Bitcoin deliberately left out — contracts that settle in the scarce asset itself. Here is exactly what changed, and what it cost.

identical.heading: What is identical
identical.tagline: Bitcoin's monetary constitution, adopted whole. These are constants, not policies.

items.title: 21,000,000 coins, halving schedule and all
items.description: A 50 LAX subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks, converging on 21 million — Bitcoin's schedule to the coin. The schedule is the entire monetary history, past and future. It does not respond to adoption, to crisis, or to argument.

items.title: Proof-of-work at ten-minute blocks
items.description: Nakamoto consensus with a 600-second target. At ten minutes, propagation is a negligible fraction of the interval, proximity advantages approach zero, and a modest machine on a residential connection verifies the chain as authoritatively as any industrial operation.

items.title: A fair launch you can check
items.description: Source code public before launch, launch date announced in advance, supply at genesis: zero. The genesis block embeds a launch-day newspaper headline, exactly as Bitcoin's did — the chain could not have been constructed before the news.

items.title: 100-block coinbase maturity
items.description: Newly mined coins are spendable only after 100 more blocks are built on top of them. A miner's revenue is bound to the permanence of the chain they extend — honesty by arithmetic, not ethics.

items.title: Fees to miners, nothing burned
items.description: A first-price auction, paid to the miner in full. Fee revenue is the network's entire security budget once the subsidy decays; a protocol that burns fees is purchasing present scarcity with its future defense.

different.heading: What is different — and why
different.tagline: Four deliberate departures, each with its reasoning on record.

items.title: The EVM, complete through Paris
items.description: Credit, exchange, escrow — every instrument historically built atop scarce money can be built here without a custodian, a wrapper, or a peg. Contracts hold, move, and settle the base asset directly: agreements that execute exactly as written, against money that cannot be diluted.

items.title: Accounts instead of UTXOs
items.description: Balances live under secp256k1 keys with Ethereum-style addresses, so existing key infrastructure — hardware signers included — operates unchanged. The trade-off is candidly stated: the account model makes address reuse the path of least resistance, and reuse links activity. Treat addresses as disposable where privacy matters.

items.title: ASERT difficulty, adjusted every block
items.description: Parallax launched with Bitcoin's 2016-block retarget. Under a severe hashrate decline the window proved manipulable, and the network migrated to ASERT at block 17,560. Both the flaw and its repair are recorded on-chain — a protocol that hides its scars is asking to be trusted. Parallax asks only to be verified.

items.title: XHash instead of SHA-256
items.description: Memory-hard and Ethash-derived, altered precisely so the existing stock of Ethash ASICs cannot be reused. A proof-of-work network is most fragile in its early years; XHash ensures security in those years is supplied by widely held GPUs rather than by whoever owns the residue of another chain's arms race.

caveats.heading: What you should be skeptical about
caveats.tagline: The honest ledger of a young chain. Verify everything; discount anything we cannot show you.

items.title: It is young
items.description: Mainnet launched October 28, 2025. Hashrate, node count, and liquidity are a fraction of Bitcoin's, and reorganizations are correspondingly cheaper — wait more confirmations for large amounts. Time is the filter, and Parallax has not yet passed through much of it.

items.title: Provenance, stated plainly
items.description: Consensus, mining, and difficulty adjustment are original, clean-room work. The EVM execution layer is reused from go-ethereum — deliberately: a battle-tested interpreter over a novel one. Anyone claiming Parallax shares no code with other chains would be wrong, so we do not claim it.

items.title: Not a Bitcoin replacement
items.description: Parallax regards Bitcoin as the ultimate form of digital sound money. This is a complementary experiment — extending Bitcoin's monetary discipline into a programmable environment — with its own risks. If what you want is money at rest, Bitcoin already exists.

parallaxForDevelopers.pageSubtitle: Your stack works — Solidity, Hardhat, Foundry, MetaMask — with a chain ID change and one compiler flag. What changes is the ground under your contract: monetary rules and consensus that cannot be governance-voted out from under it.

rows.label: Fee model
rows.value: First-price gas auction — no base fee, no burn

config.heading: Compiler and network config
config.tagline: The one thing that will bite you: Solidity 0.8.20+ targets Shanghai by default and emits PUSH0, which Paris does not have. Pin the EVM version and everything else is ordinary.

differences.heading: What is different from Ethereum mainnet
differences.tagline: Five differences that change how you design, none that change how you write Solidity.

items.title: Probabilistic finality
items.description: Proof-of-work has no finality checkpoints. Treat six confirmations (~1 hour) as settlement for high-value flows, fewer for small ones — and design your UX around pending states.

items.title: Ten-minute blocks
items.description: Inclusion takes minutes, not seconds. Batch operations, precompute what you can, and lean on events with optimistic UI. Sub-second UX belongs in layers built above settlement — which the EVM makes possible here.

items.title: Legacy fee market
items.description: A first-price gas auction: set gasPrice directly. There is no base fee and no EIP-1559 estimation — fee logic written for mainnet's fee market needs a legacy pricing path.

items.title: Paris-level EVM
items.description: No PUSH0, no transient storage (EIP-1153), no MCOPY, no blobs (EIP-4844). Everything through Paris behaves exactly as on mainnet — the semantics your audited dependencies were originally written against.

items.title: No scheduled forks
items.description: There is no upgrade cadence and no deprecation treadmill. The execution environment you deploy against is intended to stay — ossification is the feature, and your contract's assumptions age well because the ground does not move.

why.heading: Why build on a proof-of-work base layer
why.body: Every instrument historically built atop scarce money — credit, exchange, custody, derivatives — settles somewhere. On Parallax it settles against a base asset with a fixed supply, secured by physical work, on a chain with no foundation, no token vote, and no mechanism by which a transaction can be privileged or refused. Your contract inherits that neutrality: no one can be stopped from deploying, and nothing deployed can be stopped.

verify.pageSubtitle: Parallax asks for no belief. Every claim on this site can be checked against the chain itself — these are the commands.

genesis.heading: The genesis block
genesis.body1: The chain began on October 28, 2025 with a minimal genesis: no premine, no pre-deployed contracts, no privileged accounts. Embedded in its extra-data field is a newspaper headline from launch day:
genesis.headline: The Times 28/Oct/2025 Trump tells Japan: Any favours you need, we'll be there
genesis.body2: A chain constructed in secret before the announced launch could not contain news from launch day. Ask any node for block zero and check both the hash and the headline:
genesis.cmdHashLabel: Fetch block zero and its hash

supply.heading: The supply
supply.body1: Supply at genesis was zero. Every LAX in existence was mined afterward at 50 per block, halving every 210,000 blocks — so the correct total supply at any height is computable by hand, and any deviation would be a consensus violation every node rejects.
supply.body2: Nothing here needs this website. Compute the supply from any node's block height, or ask your own node, which keeps the same sum itself. Start it with --http --http.api eth,net,web3,xhash for the second command; the public RPC doesn't expose that namespace.
supply.cmdComputedLabel: Compute it from the block height (any node, including the public RPC)
supply.cmdNodeLabel: Ask your own node (total supply in wei)

rules.heading: The rules
rules.body1: Chain ID 2110. Ten-minute target interval. A 600M gas limit adjustable by at most ±0.1% per block. Do not take this page's word for any of it — ask the network:
rules.cmdBlockLabel: Latest block — check timestamp spacing and gas limit

node.heading: Don't trust this page
node.body1: Every command above points at a public RPC endpoint for convenience — but a convenient endpoint is a trusted third party. The client runs on any commodity machine; sync your own node and point the same commands at localhost. That is the entire design: verification belongs to anyone with a modest computer, and this website is not part of the trust model.

mining.title: Mining Parallax
mining.subtitle: Every coin in existence was mined, and every coin ever issued will be. Miners are the network's security budget — and if you kept an Ethash-class GPU rig, it still works.

rig.heading: Your old Ethereum rig works
rig.body: XHash is Ethash-derived: memory-hard, GPU-competitive, and altered precisely so that the existing stock of Ethash ASICs cannot be reused. Your GPUs carry over — the software changes: mine with Hashwarp, the official open-source miner, or with SRBMiner-Multi. Epochs are shortened to 720 blocks (about five days per DAG regeneration at ten-minute blocks).

rows.value: Paid to miners in full — nothing burned

mine.title: Mine LAX
mine.description: Blocks are found with XHash, a GPU proof of work. Use Hashwarp, the official miner, or SRBMiner-Multi — ethminer and other legacy Ethash miners will not work. Every transaction fee goes to the miner who finds the block.

bootnode.title: Run a bootnode
bootnode.description: Bootnodes introduce new nodes to their first peers. A good one is always on, has a stable public IP and keeps port 32110 TCP/UDP open. Share its enode address (admin.nodeInfo in the console) so others can pass it to --bootnodes.

rpc.title: Run a public RPC
rpc.description: Wallets and apps need an endpoint to talk to. Start the node with --http, expose only the eth, net and web3 namespaces, put it behind a reverse proxy with rate limits, and never keep an unlocked account on it.

build.title: Build
build.description: Parallax runs the EVM through Paris, with Ethereum-format addresses. The tools you already use work.

evm.title: Build on the EVM
evm.description: Deploy with Solidity, Hardhat, Foundry and MetaMask against chain ID 2110 and https://rpc.parallaxprotocol.org. Pin the compiler's EVM version to paris — Solidity 0.8.20+ emits PUSH0 by default. There is no EIP-1559: set a legacy gas price.

client.title: Contribute to the client
client.description: The node, the miner and the tooling are developed in the open. Pick an issue, open a pull request, or review someone else's. Contributions are judged on correctness, not credentials.

parallaxClient.title: Run a Parallax node
parallaxClient.subtitle: The Parallax Client is the reference node software. Run parallaxd and check every block against Parallax's rules yourself, on Linux, macOS, Windows or in Docker.

header.walletLink: Parallax Wallet runs a full node too

fullNode.heading: What a full node does
fullNode.subtitle: A full node downloads every block and checks every transaction against the rules itself. It trusts no one, miners included.

decentralized.heading: Decentralized
decentralized.body: Node operators keep Parallax decentralized. They individually run their own Parallax full nodes, and each of those full nodes separately follows the exact same rules to decide which block chain is valid.

noVoting.heading: No voting
noVoting.body: There's no voting or other corruptible process involved: there's just individual software following identical rules—"math"—to evaluate identical blocks and coming to identical conclusions about which block chain is valid.

fullNode.blockquote: This shared agreement (called consensus) allows people like you to only accept valid transactions, enforcing Parallax's rules against even the most powerful miners.

verify.title: Verify, don't trust
verify.description: Your node checks every block, signature and proof of work against the rules, the 21,000,000 LAX cap among them. A wallet pointed at it sees the chain as it is, not as a server reports it.

privacy.title: Keep your lookups private
privacy.description: A public RPC sees which addresses you ask about. Point your wallet at your own node and those questions never leave your computer.

network.title: Strengthen the network
network.description: Every independent node is one more copy of the rules that a bad block has to get past. Open port 32110 (TCP and UDP) and your node also serves the chain to new peers.

build.title: Build on it
build.description: parallaxd serves JSON-RPC over HTTP, WebSocket and IPC for your own apps and scripts. Keep it on your machine or network; never expose an unauthenticated RPC port to the internet.

binaries.heading: Four programs in every archive
binaries.subtitle: Every release archive holds the same command-line tools. Each does one job.

items.parallaxd: The full-node daemon. Runs a full or archive node and serves JSON-RPC over HTTP, WebSocket and IPC.
items.parallax-cli: The command-line RPC client, with short commands like info, peers, balance and sendraw. It finds your node's IPC socket on its own.
items.parallax-wallet: An offline wallet tool: create, list and import accounts, and sign messages and transactions. It never talks to a running node.
items.parallax: A multi-call wrapper: parallax node, parallax rpc and parallax wallet run the three above.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.subtitle: This site is built to know as little about you as possible.
privacy.intro: parallaxprotocol.org is an informational site. It has no user accounts, runs no analytics or advertising, sets no tracking cookies, and never sells or shares visitor data — nothing of the kind is collected in the first place. That is also why there is no cookie banner: nothing on this site requires consent. This page describes the little that does happen when you visit.

browser.title: What your browser stores
browser.body: The site sets a single cookie, NEXT_LOCALE, to remember your language so pages load in the right one. It also uses your browser's local storage for small interface preferences — for example, remembering that you already dismissed the wallet-network prompt. Neither identifies you nor tracks you across sites, and you can clear both in your browser settings at any time.

hosting.title: Hosting and server logs
hosting.body: The site is served through Cloudflare's content delivery network. Like any web server, it transiently processes standard technical data — your IP address, the requested URL, and browser headers — to deliver pages and defend against abuse. No analytics run on top of this data.

external.title: External content
external.body1: Market data is fetched by our servers, so your browser never contacts CoinGecko. Live network statistics load from our own block explorer at explorer.parallaxprotocol.org.
external.body2: Embedded YouTube videos are click-to-play: until you press play, only a static thumbnail image is loaded from Google's servers. Pressing play loads the video in YouTube's privacy-enhanced mode, at which point Google's privacy policy applies.

hero.title: Your own node and your own keys, in one app
hero.subtitle: Parallax Wallet runs a complete Parallax node, keeps your keys sealed under one password, signs on a Ledger, a Trezor or an air-gapped computer, and lets an AI assistant help without ever touching a key.

node.heading: A full node, built in
node.subtitle: The app runs a complete Parallax node inside its own process. No separate install, no sidecar, and no server between you and the chain.

own.title: Balances from your own chain
own.description: Balances, history and fees come from your own copy of the chain, checked block by block, not from someone else's server.

history.title: Every transaction, indexed on your disk
history.description: The app keeps its own index of the chain, so an account's whole history loads in a few lookups, and an account you import has its history at once, with no rescan.

network.title: The network at a glance
network.description: A block clock against the 10-minute target, sync progress, the latest blocks, your connected peers and the mempool.

inbound.title: It helps the network
inbound.description: By default the node accepts connections from other peers on port 32110 and maps it on your router by UPnP or NAT-PMP. Prefer outbound only? It's one switch.

diagram.rpc: Local HTTP-RPC on 127.0.0.1, for your own tools. Never exposed to the network, and the wallet doesn't need it.

security.heading: Sealed by default
security.subtitle: Built on the node's own key management and established libraries, not new cryptography.

password.title: One password
password.description: Every key and recovery phrase is encrypted with your wallet password. Unlock once; the wallet locks itself after 15 idle minutes by default, and whenever the computer sleeps.

keystore.title: Standard keystore files
keystore.description: One Web3 Secret Storage file per key (scrypt, AES-128-CTR), the format parallaxd and the parallax-wallet tool use. Kept apart from the chain data and never attached to the node, so nothing that connects to its RPC can use them.

sealed.title: Everything else, sealed
sealed.description: Account names, contacts, watch-only accounts, signing records and pending sends are sealed with XChaCha20-Poly1305, each file bound to its name. A locked wallet doesn't even reveal how many accounts it holds.

moment.title: A key only for the moment
moment.description: A key is decrypted for the one action that needs it, then wiped. While the wallet is unlocked, the password is held sealed in memory kept out of swap and core dumps.

confirm.title: The dangerous steps ask again
confirm.description: Revealing a recovery phrase, saving a backup, removing a key and changing the password always take the password typed again. A new phrase is confirmed by retyping three of its words.

local.title: Crash reports stay on your disk
local.description: Crash reports are written to your own config folder and never sent anywhere. Fonts ship with the app, so it makes no third-party requests to draw itself.

platform.heading: Memory protection, by platform

rows.guarded: The password and wallet key are held in locked, guarded memory while the wallet is unlocked
rows.dumps: No core dump is written if the app crashes
rows.attach: Other programs running as you can't read the app's memory
rows.erase: Memory used while signing is wiped afterwards

platform.note: Windows has nothing like Linux's non-dumpable flag. There, your keys are protected by the encryption and the locked memory above.

signing.heading: Keys that never touch this computer
signing.subtitle: Keep a key on a hardware wallet, or on a computer that never goes online. The app prepares the transaction; the key signs where it lives.

hardware.label: Hardware wallets
hardware.title: Ledger and Trezor
hardware.description: Accounts whose keys stay on the device. Every send, signed message and assistant request is confirmed on the device's own screen, with no wallet password.
points: Bring accounts in from Settings: the app finds them along the standard and Ledger Live paths.
A replacement restored from the same recovery phrase signs too. A device holding a different wallet is caught before it's asked to sign.
Check a receiving address on the device's screen.
On Linux, the app installs the USB rules the devices need.

offline.label: Air-gapped
offline.title: Offline signing, by QR code or file
offline.description: Run Parallax Wallet as an offline signer on a computer that never connects: its node never starts and it never checks for updates. Your everyday wallet follows the same accounts as watch-only.

prepare.title: Prepare
prepare.description: The online wallet builds a signing request with the nonce, fee and gas only its node knows.

sign.title: Sign
sign.description: The offline signer scans the QR code or opens the file, shows exactly what would be signed, and signs. A fee cap, 1 LAX by default, refuses anything above it.

broadcast.title: Broadcast
broadcast.description: The signed transaction comes back the same way and is checked against the request before it's broadcast.

offline.note: Messages can be signed offline too. The request format is shared with the parallax-wallet command-line tool.

assistant.heading: An assistant that never touches a key
assistant.subtitle: Parallax Wallet runs its own MCP server, so Claude or any MCP client can read the chain through your node and, as far as you allow, help with your wallet.

permissions.title: You decide what it may do
permissions.description: Every feature is set to Allow, Ask or Block: node status and logs, your accounts and activity, contacts, starting or stopping the node, settings, new accounts and sends. Ask is the default for nearly all of them.

sends.title: Every send approved by you
sends.description: An assistant can prepare a send. It goes only after you review it in the app and enter your wallet password, or confirm it on your hardware wallet.

local.title: Answered by your own node
local.description: Chain data comes from your node, not a public RPC. The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, needs its access token, and refuses requests from web pages. The public explorer and status page stay off unless you turn them on.

lock.title: It can lock, never unlock
lock.description: An assistant can lock the app, as its lock button does. Only you can unlock it, and while it's locked the assistant can do nothing.

never.heading: No assistant can, whatever you allow
items: Export, import or back up keys
See or change the wallet password
Sign or send without your approval
Open the node to the network

connect.label: Connect Claude Code
connect.note: Settings › AI assistants shows the address and your token, and a JSON config for any other MCP client.
connect.guide: Set up an assistant, step by step

everyday.heading: Everything else a wallet should do
everyday.subtitle: The daily work, done carefully.

send.title: Send, with a full review
send.description: The whole recipient address, the amount, the fee and the total before you sign. Your contacts and your own accounts are named. Speed up or cancel a send that's still waiting.

receive.title: Receive with a QR code
receive.description: Your address and its QR code, which you can check on a hardware wallet's screen.

history.title: Complete history
history.description: Every transaction and mined block of every account. Search, filter by received, sent, mined or failed, jump to a date or a block, and export to CSV.

contacts.title: Contacts
contacts.description: Names for the addresses you pay, sealed like the rest. Each name and address is unique, so a look-alike entry can't hide behind a familiar one.

messages.title: Sign and verify messages
messages.description: Prove you control an address with a standard EIP-191 signature, and check anyone else's.

phrases.title: Several recovery phrases
phrases.description: 24 words by default, with an optional passphrase. Accounts follow MetaMask's derivation path, so the same words restore the same accounts there; imports also scan the Ledger Live and legacy paths.

watchOnly.title: Watch-only accounts
watchOnly.description: Follow any address's balance and history, or pair it with an offline signer to send from it.

mining.title: Mining rewards
mining.description: Blocks you mined show in your history with their reward, their fees and when they can be spent.

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.description: When LAX arrives, when a send confirms or fails, when a long sync finishes, and if the node stops because the disk is nearly full.

updates.title: Verified updates
updates.description: The app checks for new releases and verifies each download's SHA-256 checksum before installing it. Background checks can be turned off.

languages.title: Seven languages
languages.description: English, Deutsch, Français, Português (Brasil), Русский, 中文（新加坡） and 中文（繁體）.

themes.title: Light and dark
themes.description: Follows your system, or pick one.

upcoming.heading: What's being built
upcoming.subtitle: Not in the app yet. Both are being built for Parallax Wallet now.

stealth.title: Stealth addresses
stealth.description: Share one address publicly while every payment lands at a fresh one that outside observers can't link back to you.

channels.title: Payment channels
channels.description: Instant LAX payments signed off-chain and carried end-to-end encrypted over Nostr relays, with no payment servers. They even work with no internet, in three QR scans.
